title: Suspicious LSASS Memory-Read Access
exclusions: This rule identifies Sysmon ProcessAccess events whose target ends in `\lsass.exe` and whose exact normalized `GrantedAccess` value is `0x1010` or `0x1410`. It does not prove that memory was read successfully, that a dump was created, that credentials were recovered, or that the source process is malicious. It intentionally does not match query-only `0x1000`, broader read/write masks such as `0x1438` or `0x143a`, full-access values such as `0x1fffff`, kernel-mode access invisible to this telemetry, offline dump parsing, registry/SAM/NTDS credential dumping, DCSync, Security Support Provider changes, or hosts where Sysmon Event ID 10 was not generated or collected. Protected Process Light and Credential Guard can affect attacker behavior but are not inferred from this event. The catalogue SPL contains no process-name allowlist or exception lookup; any deployment suppression must be narrowly validated. This documentation-only review makes no runtime, malware-execution, prevention, attribution, or regulatory-assurance claim.
evidence: After deployment, retain the version-controlled `windows_lsass_memory_read_access` saved-search definition and ACL; its cron, dispatch, and triggered-alert history; every result row with endpoint, source/target process identifiers, exact access mask and decoded rights, first/last seen time, event count, call trace, source, and source type; the corresponding raw Sysmon Event ID 10 XML and EventRecordID; the effective Sysmon configuration showing the `ProcessAccess` rule; the effective Splunk WinEventLog input and Splunk Add-on for Sysmon version; source-health evidence; dated positive and negative control results; alert delivery evidence; investigation disposition; and any approved, bounded suppression record. This review produced no Sysmon event, Splunk search job, alert, memory dump, or production evidence.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated test index, place one XML event at a fixed time inside the closed five-minute search window with `source=XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational`, `sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog`, `EventCode=10`, `Computer=WIN-LAB01.example`, `SourceImage=C:\Lab\reader.exe`, `SourceProcessId=4242`, `SourceProcessGUID={11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111}`, `TargetImage=C:\Windows\System32\lsass.exe`, `TargetProcessId=700`, `GrantedAccess=0x1010`, and a nonempty `CallTrace`. Expect exactly one row with `endpoint=win-lab01.example`, `event_count=1`, `granted_access=0x1010`, and `access_rights=PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION + PROCESS_VM_READ`. Repeat with uppercase `0X1410`; expect normalization to `0x1410` and the three-right decode. Documentation review checks this logic but does not claim the fixture was replayed.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Run isolated variants and expect zero rows for each: Event ID 10 targeting `notepad.exe` with `0x1010`; LSASS targeted with query-only `0x1000`; LSASS targeted with broader `0x1438`; Event ID 1 with otherwise identical fields; an event outside the delayed closed five-minute window; and a row with an empty endpoint or source image. Also place two in-window `0x1010` events with the same endpoint, source process GUID, target process ID, and source image; before alerting, expect one grouped row with `event_count=2`, proving that count is aggregation rather than a threshold.

dataSources: Microsoft Sysmon ProcessAccess Event ID 10 from `Applications and Services Logs/Microsoft/Windows/Sysmon/Operational`, collected directly by a Splunk forwarder in XML form. The deployment-local index is `wineventlog`; the supported primary contract is `sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog` and `source=XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational`. Splunk Add-on for Sysmon (Splunkbase 5709) supplies supported parsing and knowledge. Required native fields are `EventCode`/`EventID`, `Computer`, `SourceImage`, `SourceProcessId`, `SourceProcessGUID`, `TargetImage`, `TargetProcessId`, `TargetProcessGUID`, `GrantedAccess`, and `CallTrace`; `dest` and `host` are endpoint fallbacks. Event ID 10 exists only when the active Sysmon configuration includes the relevant `ProcessAccess` target. WEF/WEC collection requires a separately validated dedicated channel and source identity.
app: Splunk Add-on for Sysmon (`Splunk_TA_microsoft_sysmon`, Splunkbase 5709), version 5.0.1, with a currently supported Microsoft Sysmon binary and Splunk platform combination. Install collection inputs on endpoint forwarders or the designated WEC collector and deploy parsing/search-time knowledge to the tiers required by the topology. Splunk documents that Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows is not required for this add-on to function. No premium Splunk app is required.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog" source="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" EventCode=10 earliest=-10m@m latest=-5m@m
| eval event_code=tonumber(coalesce(EventCode,EventID)), endpoint=lower(trim(coalesce(dest,Computer,host))), source_image=trim(SourceImage), source_process_id=trim(SourceProcessId), source_process_guid=trim(SourceProcessGUID), target_image=trim(TargetImage), target_process_id=trim(TargetProcessId), target_process_guid=trim(TargetProcessGUID), granted_access=lower(trim(GrantedAccess))
| where event_code=10 AND match(target_image,"(?i)\\\\lsass\.exe$") AND in(granted_access,"0x1010","0x1410") AND len(endpoint)>0 AND len(source_image)>0
| stats count as event_count min(_time) as first_seen max(_time) as last_seen values(CallTrace) as call_trace values(source) as observed_sources values(sourcetype) as observed_sourcetypes by endpoint source_image source_process_id source_process_guid target_image target_process_id target_process_guid granted_access
| eval access_rights=case(granted_access="0x1010","PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION + PROCESS_VM_READ",granted_access="0x1410","PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION + PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION + PROCESS_VM_READ"), detection_reason="LSASS target with an exact memory-read access mask"
| table first_seen last_seen endpoint source_image source_process_id source_process_guid target_image target_process_id target_process_guid granted_access access_rights event_count call_trace observed_sources observed_sourcetypes detection_reason
| sort 0 -last_seen endpoint source_image
description: Reports each endpoint/source-process group in a delayed, closed five-minute window when Sysmon Event ID 10 records access to `lsass.exe` with exact mask `0x1010` or `0x1410`. Both masks include `PROCESS_VM_READ`; the latter also includes both documented query rights. A row is a high-priority memory-access lead, not proof that credential dumping succeeded.
value: Unexpected read access to the Local Security Authority process can precede theft of reusable credentials, hashes, or tickets that enable privilege escalation and lateral movement. Preserving source process identity, target identity, mask, and call trace lets responders contain a potentially compromised Windows host quickly while distinguishing security tooling and approved tests from adversary behavior.
implementation: Configure Microsoft Sysmon to generate ProcessAccess Event ID 10 for targets ending in `\lsass.exe`, collect the channel as XML into the local `wineventlog` index, and verify the Splunk Add-on for Sysmon fields before enabling the alert. Save the SPL as `windows_lsass_memory_read_access`, run it every five minutes for the preceding delayed closed bucket, and trigger on any row. Treat `0x1010` and `0x1410` as exact bitmasks containing memory-read rights, not as unique Mimikatz signatures; investigate every source and use only evidence-backed, expiring suppressions.
visualization: On a restricted Windows credential-access dashboard, place source-health and Event ID 10 volume panels first. Follow with a single value for distinct affected endpoints over 24 hours; a timechart of `event_count` split by `source_image`; and a drilldown table showing `first_seen`, `last_seen`, `endpoint`, `source_image`, source/target process IDs and GUIDs, `granted_access`, `access_rights`, `event_count`, and `call_trace`. Default the analyst picker to 24 hours, link a row to the exact raw EventRecordID window and adjacent Sysmon process/file events, and never label a result as confirmed credential theft.
schema: Microsoft Sysmon Event ID 10 native XML fields enriched by Splunk Add-on for Sysmon
dataModelAcceleration: No CIM accelerated substitute is claimed. The Splunk Add-on for Sysmon documents broad CIM mappings, but its current source documentation does not map Event ID 10's source-to-target process-access relationship, `GrantedAccess`, and `CallTrace` to a CIM dataset that preserves this rule. `Endpoint.Processes` describes process inventory/creation and cannot prove that one process opened LSASS with a particular mask. At scale, use a governed summary of the exact native fields only after raw-versus-summary parity tests.

knownFalsePositives:
A matching event is real process-handle access under the documented mask contract. “False positive” here means authorized or expected access rather than a fabricated event.

1. **Microsoft Defender for Endpoint or another approved EDR/antimalware sensor** — A credential-protection or inspection component may open LSASS. Do not allowlist a vendor name from assumption. Establish the exact signed binary path, signer, hash/version, service, expected `GrantedAccess`, stable `CallTrace`, deployment ring, and matching EDR health/change evidence on representative hosts. Suppress only that measured tuple and expire it at the product upgrade or policy-review date.

2. **Sysinternals Process Explorer used by an administrator** — Elevated process inspection can query protected processes and may produce one of the selected masks. Correlate `SourceImage` with the approved Process Explorer path and Authenticode signer, interactive logon/session, administrator identity, support ticket, and short activity interval. Use a time-bounded exception for the named host and signed hash; never suppress all `procexp*.exe` paths indefinitely.

3. **Approved Microsoft Sysinternals ProcDump or Task Manager LSASS collection during incident response** — A responder-created dump is intentionally the behavior this rule protects. Require an incident number, named responder, exact UTC window, source process hash, adjacent process-creation evidence, expected dump path/file event, chain-of-custody record, and secure deletion/retention decision. Keep the detection as test or investigation evidence and suppress only duplicate notification for that case.

4. **Atomic Red Team, adversary-emulation, or purple-team credential-access exercise** — A controlled T1003.001 test should alert. Distinguish it with the approved exercise plan, isolated assets, operator, expected source hash/command, UTC bounds, and downstream containment safeguards. Apply an expiring notification exception keyed to endpoint and exercise ID after the base search; never remove the event from dashboards or evidence.

5. **Vendor support or credential-provider diagnostic utility** — Identity, smart-card, single-sign-on, PAM, or authentication support tooling may inspect LSASS in a vendor-directed session. Confirm the vendor case, signed package provenance, exact command, source process hash, operator, affected host, and expected call trace. Treat an unsigned, user-writable, renamed, or newly observed binary as suspicious even if its file name resembles the approved utility.

**Safe suppression:** preserve the base result. If notification tuning is necessary, use an access-controlled lookup keyed by exact `endpoint,source_image,source_hash,granted_access,call_trace_fingerprint` with owner, approver, ticket, numeric `valid_from_epoch`, and exclusive `valid_until_epoch`. Apply it only in an alert wrapper, reject wildcards/open-ended rows, and revalidate after Sysmon, Windows, EDR, or tool upgrades.
reviewer: documentation-only Cursor AI editorial review against Microsoft Sysmon and Win32 process-access documentation, Splunk Add-on for Sysmon and Splunk Security Content, and MITRE ATT&CK; Sysmon configuration, event generation, SPL, tests, alert delivery, suppression tuples, scale, and production response not executed or SME-signed

cost.search_load_notes: The five-minute raw search is narrow, but ProcessAccess ingest can be substantial if Sysmon is not filtered at the target. Search cost stays low when Event ID 10 generation is scoped to LSASS and the source/index predicates are retained.

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and detection contract

Assign a SOC detection owner, Windows/Sysmon configuration owner, Splunk data owner, incident responder, and exception approver. Deploy a currently supported Microsoft Sysmon binary using a security-reviewed XML configuration. Install Splunk Add-on for Sysmon (`Splunk_TA_microsoft_sysmon`, Splunkbase 5709) 5.0.1 on the Splunk tiers required by the documented topology, and qualify that exact add-on, Sysmon, Windows, forwarder, and Splunk combination outside production. Splunkbase lists add-on 5.0.1 for Splunk Enterprise 9.2 through current 10.x releases and Splunk Cloud at review time; recheck compatibility before deployment. Splunk documents that its Microsoft Windows add-on is not required for the Sysmon add-on to function.

The endpoint collection service must be able to read `Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational` and forward to the approved receivers. The search role needs read access to the deployment-local `wineventlog` index and permission to save and schedule this search. Restrict raw Sysmon access because process paths, user context, and call traces can reveal security tooling and investigative activity. Do not grant local administrator, process-debug, host-isolation, lookup-write, or response permissions merely to run the detection.

Define the signal precisely. Sysmon Event ID 10 records that one process opened another and reports the access flags in `GrantedAccess`; it does not state that every requested operation occurred or that credential material was obtained. `0x1010` is the sum of Microsoft's `PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION` (`0x1000`) and `PROCESS_VM_READ` (`0x0010`). `0x1410` adds `PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION` (`0x0400`). These values are bitmasks, not unique Mimikatz signatures. Splunk Security Content uses the exact two values for an LSASS-access analytic, while also requiring extensive triage.

This UC deliberately favors that narrow documented contract. It does not match every mask that contains `PROCESS_VM_READ`; for example `0x1438` adds VM operation/write rights, and `0x143a` also adds create-thread. It also does not match `PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS`. Broader hunts can be valuable but have a different noise and testing contract. Any mask expansion must be decoded against Microsoft access-right constants, replayed against fleet telemetry, and reflected in tests, prose, dashboard labels, and suppressions.

## Step 1 — Configure Sysmon and XML collection

Inspect the active Sysmon schema with the same deployed executable (`Sysmon64.exe -s` or its 32-bit equivalent) and inspect the active configuration with `Sysmon64.exe -c`. Merge a targeted ProcessAccess include into the governed configuration rather than replacing unrelated rules:

```xml
<Sysmon schemaversion="4.82">
  <EventFiltering>
    <ProcessAccess onmatch="include">
      <TargetImage condition="end with">\lsass.exe</TargetImage>
    </ProcessAccess>
  </EventFiltering>
</Sysmon>
```

The schema version shown is an example, not a required binary version; use the schema emitted by the deployed Sysmon executable. Apply an updated file with `Sysmon64.exe -c C:\ProgramData\Sysmon\sysmon-config.xml`. Avoid uninstall/reinstall as a routine configuration update. Confirm Event Viewer exposes **Applications and Services Logs > Microsoft > Windows > Sysmon > Operational**, and confirm Sysmon configuration-change events identify the intended revision. Microsoft warns that ProcessAccess can be noisy and recommends targeted filtering.

For direct collection, deploy a local WinEventLog input through the managed forwarder configuration:

```ini
[WinEventLog://Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational]
disabled = 0
renderXml = true
index = wineventlog
current_only = 1
checkpointInterval = 5
```

`wineventlog` is this catalogue's deployment choice, not a vendor-mandated index. XML is required for the documented `sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog` and `source=XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational` contract. `current_only=1` is appropriate for a new live feed only when historical backfill is not required; record any different checkpoint/start policy because replayed history changes test and alert interpretation. Use a separate deployment app for local input choices so add-on upgrades do not overwrite them.

If WEF/WEC is used, follow the Sysmon add-on's dedicated-channel guidance and validate the `WEC-Sysmon` input separately. Do not silently point the primary SPL at a collector channel: prove original endpoint identity, source/source-type naming, field extraction, latency, duplicate prevention, and capacity first. High-volume Sysmon forwarding can stress collectors.

Verify one raw Event ID 10 event before enabling the alert:

```spl
index=wineventlog sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog" source="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" EventCode=10 earliest=-24h
| fieldsummary
| search field IN (Computer,SourceImage,SourceProcessId,SourceProcessGUID,TargetImage,TargetProcessId,TargetProcessGUID,GrantedAccess,CallTrace)
```

Require stable endpoint identity and nonempty source image, target image, mask, and process identifiers. Compare the raw XML names with Splunk Security Content's Event ID 10 data-source record. Confirm source health separately with counts by host and EventCode; a silent host is unknown, not clean.

## Step 2 — Create and understand the saved search

Save the catalogue SPL as `windows_lsass_memory_read_access`. Schedule it every five minutes, for example `*/5 * * * *`, and trigger when result count is greater than zero. The search examines the closed bucket from ten to five minutes before the search boundary. The five-minute delay is a starting allowance for indexing latency; measure p95/p99 delay and increase it if valid events arrive later. If the delay changes, keep windows nonoverlapping or document intentional overlap and deduplication.

The base predicates constrain index, XML source type, exact Sysmon channel source, and Event ID before transforming data. `coalesce(dest,Computer,host)` acknowledges supported enrichment and native XML while preserving a last-resort Splunk metadata fallback. The `match` expression requires the target path to end in `\lsass.exe`, case-insensitively; it does not match a lookalike suffix. Lowercasing `GrantedAccess` makes `0X1410` and `0x1410` equivalent without converting the hexadecimal string to an unverified number.

`stats` creates one result per endpoint, source process identity, target process identity, and mask. `event_count` is context, not a trigger threshold: one qualifying handle access is enough. Process GUIDs are retained because process IDs are reusable. `CallTrace` remains investigative evidence and can distinguish stable product behavior, but a DLL name in a trace is not proof of maliciousness. The final decode is declarative for only the two admitted masks.

Do not copy the former blanket exclusions for `MsMpEng`, `csrss`, `wininit`, `svchost`, or filename-only tools. A trusted name can be renamed or abused, product behavior changes, and a broad exclusion can hide the event the rule exists to preserve. If notification volume requires tuning, use the bounded post-search mechanism in `knownFalsePositives`; keep the base search and dashboard unsuppressed.

No CIM `tstats` variant is supplied. `Endpoint.Processes` can show that a process exists or was created, but cannot reproduce source process opening target LSASS with the native mask and call trace. For scale, first constrain Event ID 10 at Sysmon. Only then consider a summary index carrying every grouping and evidence field, plus source-health/completeness metadata.

## Step 3 — Validate fields, exact masks, windows, and controls

Use synthetic XML in an isolated index to execute the positive and negative scenarios. Fix the search boundary or substitute fixed epoch bounds during assertions so `now()` cannot move. Assert exact result count, normalized endpoint, normalized mask, access-right text, source/target IDs and GUIDs, and grouped event count. Test uppercase mask input. Test path case and both `System32` and legitimate alternate path casing, while rejecting `lsass.exe.bak` and non-LSASS targets.

Boundary-test `_time` immediately before, at, and after `earliest` and `latest`; Splunk's latest bound is exclusive. Verify delayed late arrivals deliberately rather than assuming five minutes is sufficient. Test duplicate collection through direct and WEF paths and ensure the same native EventRecordID is not counted twice. Test missing `dest` with valid `Computer`, then missing both with `host`, and reject empty endpoint identity.

Compare two source events with Event Viewer XML on the originating host. Confirm `EventID=10`, Computer, source and target process GUID/ID, image paths, GrantedAccess, CallTrace, UTC event time, and EventRecordID. Then compare the active configuration output to the version-controlled XML. A raw event with unexpected field names or source metadata is an integration defect; do not paper over it with guessed aliases.

Run a 24-hour source-health check by endpoint and EventCode. Expected hosts with no recent Sysmon service/configuration/process events require collection investigation. Also monitor Event ID 255 errors and configuration changes; neither is part of this trigger, but both affect confidence. Record add-on, Sysmon, Windows, forwarder, Splunk, configuration hash, test bounds, expected and actual rows, search job ID, and operator. Keep `status=draft` until runtime tests, alert delivery, source health, volume, dashboard access, suppressions, and response receive human acceptance.

## Step 4 — Operationalize triage, response, dashboards, and evidence

Build the restricted dashboard described in `visualization`. Give source-health failures equal prominence so zero detections are never presented as proof of safety. Preserve source and target GUIDs in drilldown. Correlate the source process GUID with Sysmon Event ID 1 process creation, Event IDs 7/11 for loaded images or created dump files where configured, code-signing/hash enrichment, interactive logon, EDR process telemetry, recent software deployment, and the exact incident/change system.

When a result fires: (1) verify source freshness, raw XML, endpoint identity, mask, process GUIDs, source path, signer/hash, and call trace; (2) determine whether a current approved, exact exception exists; (3) inspect process ancestry and command line from separate process-creation telemetry; (4) look for dump-file creation, archive/compression, credential use, account changes, and lateral movement; (5) contact the endpoint/EDR owner and invoke the approved credential-exposure playbook; (6) if maliciousness is plausible, preserve volatile evidence, isolate through the authorized EDR workflow, terminate only under IR authority, and reset potentially exposed credentials according to scope; and (7) document disposition and suppression feedback.

Do not automatically kill LSASS, clear Sysmon logs, delete dumps, reboot, block a signed security agent, disable Event ID 10, or reset domain-wide credentials solely from this row. LSASS termination can destabilize or restart the host, and destructive actions can remove evidence. The alert establishes a high-priority lead, not intent or successful theft.

Retain the artifacts named in `evidence` according to the organization's incident, privacy, and security-log policy. Review the two-mask policy and suppression tuples after Sysmon, Windows, EDR, credential-provider, or add-on upgrades and after red-team exercises. Track broader LSASS access as a hunt so narrow alert coverage is not mistaken for complete T1003.001 coverage.

## Step 5 — Troubleshoot product-specific failure modes

- **No Sysmon channel or events:** verify the Sysmon service/executable name, active configuration, and Event Viewer channel. Splunk's add-on troubleshooting states that a stopped Sysmon service makes the channel unavailable and recommends restarting forwarders after Sysmon resumes.
- **Event ID 10 absent while other Sysmon events exist:** inspect `Sysmon64.exe -c`; the `ProcessAccess` include may be missing, overridden by rule ordering, or not match the target path. Validate the XML against the schema from `Sysmon64.exe -s` and update with `-c`.
- **Wrong source type/source:** confirm `renderXml=true`, the direct channel stanza, and add-on deployment. The supported contract is source type `XmlWinEventLog` with the channel in `source`, not `WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational` as a modern source type.
- **Fields are null:** inspect raw XML for the native Data names and verify Splunk Add-on for Sysmon parsing/search-time knowledge reaches the relevant tiers. Do not substitute generic `Image` for `SourceImage`; it changes semantics.
- **All forwarded events show the collector:** the WEF/WEC path did not preserve or extract original `Computer`. Repair the dedicated channel/topology before enabling the alert; metadata `host` alone may identify only the collector.
- **A known test does not match:** check the exact mask. A tool can request `0x1000`, `0x1438`, `0x143a`, `0x1fffff`, or another combination rather than the two values in this rule. Record it and decide through change control whether to expand this rule or create a broader hunt.
- **Unexpected duplicate counts:** compare original Computer, EventRecordID, source, forwarder, and process GUID across direct and WEF collection. Remove duplicate routing rather than increasing a threshold.
- **Alert arrives late or misses the bucket:** compare `_time`, `_indextime`, endpoint UTC time, forwarder queues, and scheduler delay. Increase the close delay based on measured latency and rerun boundary controls.
- **High ingest or endpoint overhead:** scope ProcessAccess generation at Sysmon to LSASS targets, inspect configuration rule behavior and event rates, and test changes on canaries. Do not discard qualifying Event ID 10 records at index time merely to hide alert noise.
- **Legitimate tool floods results after upgrade:** compare signed path, hash/version, mask, and call-trace fingerprint before and after the upgrade. Expire the old tuple, document the new behavior, and obtain approval; never broaden to a filename-only wildcard.
grandmaExplanation: We notice when a program asks for permission to read the part of Windows that holds sign-in secrets. That warning helps the security team check the program quickly before stolen credentials can be used elsewhere.
hardware: Supported Windows endpoints and servers running Microsoft Sysmon with ProcessAccess Event ID 10 enabled for LSASS. Direct endpoint collection is the primary contract; WEF/WEC requires a dedicated, capacity-tested channel that preserves the original computer and native event fields.
